title: Domain IV: Procurement Business Principles - Procurement Business Principles - Disasters & Emergencies
subject: Procurement Business Principles

questions.q: What is the primary objective of a Continuity of Operations Plan (COOP) for a procurement department?
options: To ensure the agency maintains normal hours and standard bidding procedures during a catastrophic event.
To outline procedures for sustaining essential procurement functions and supply chains during and immediately after a crisis or disaster.
To completely shut down operations until FEMA arrives.
To guarantee vendors double their normal payment rate.
questions.explain: A COOP is designed to ensure that the critical, essential functions of the department continue despite a disaster, facilitating emergency response and recovery.
questions.subject: Procurement Business Principles

questions.q: Under federal FEMA reimbursement guidelines (2 CFR 200), if an agency uses an emergency sole-source procurement, what must it do as soon as the immediate exigent circumstances end?
options: Continue using the sole-source vendor for the next five years.
Transition the remaining needed goods or services to a standard competitive procurement process.
Cancel all remaining orders and return all goods.
Double the contract amount as a reward for emergency response.
questions.explain: FEMA allows noncompetitive (sole source) procurement during a declared emergency or exigency, but requires the agency to transition to a full and open competitive process as soon as the immediate threat to life, health, or safety is mitigated.
questions.subject: Procurement Business Principles

questions.q: A key difference between 'Exigency' and 'Emergency' under federal grant rules is:
options: An exigency is a threat to life, while an emergency is just a minor delay.
An emergency creates a direct threat to life, public health, or safety, whereas an exigency represents an urgent need where avoiding delay is critical, though not necessarily life-threatening.
Emergencies require competitive bidding; exigencies do not.
There is no difference in the definitions under FEMA rules.
questions.explain: FEMA differentiates between exigency (a pressing need necessitating rapid action to avoid financial or operational loss) and emergency (an immediate threat to life, safety, or property).
questions.subject: Procurement Business Principles

questions.q: To receive federal FEMA reimbursement, local agencies are generally prohibited from applying which of the following during the procurement process?
options: Evaluation criteria based on vendor experience.
Geographical preferences (e.g., 'Local Vendor Preference' statutes).
Performance bonds for construction.
Minority and Women-Owned Business Enterprise (MWBE) outreach.
questions.explain: 2 CFR 200 explicitly prohibits the use of statutorily or administratively imposed state or local geographic preferences in the evaluation of bids or proposals, except where expressly mandated by federal statute.
questions.subject: Procurement Business Principles

questions.q: Which type of contract is strictly prohibited under federal grant guidelines (including FEMA) for emergency contracting?
options: Fixed-price contracts
Time and materials (T&M) contracts
Cost-plus-a-percentage-of-cost (CPPC) contracts
Indefinite Delivery / Indefinite Quantity (IDIQ) contracts
questions.explain: Cost-plus-a-percentage-of-cost (CPPC) contracts are explicitly prohibited under federal procurement standards because they provide an incentive for the contractor to increase costs to maximize their profit.
questions.subject: Procurement Business Principles

questions.q: What is the primary benefit of 'Pre-Positioned Contracts' (also known as advance or contingency contracts)?
options: They allow the agency to pay for disaster supplies years before they are needed.
They establish competitively bid pricing and vendor commitments for emergency goods/services before a disaster strikes, ensuring rapid deployment and FEMA compliance.
They eliminate the need for an Emergency Operations Center (EOC).
They shift all financial risk entirely to the vendor.
questions.explain: Advance contracts are competitively bid during normal operations, satisfying legal requirements in advance so the agency can issue immediate task orders when disaster strikes.
questions.subject: Procurement Business Principles

questions.q: Under the FEMA reimbursement documentation guidelines, what is considered the most critical responsibility of the procurement official during an emergency response?
options: Negotiating a lower price than standard market rate.
Maintaining meticulous documentation and an audit trail of the decisions, justifications, and competitive actions taken.
Ensuring all purchases are made using petty cash.
Filing the public notice in the newspaper for 30 days.
questions.explain: Poor documentation is the leading cause of agencies losing FEMA reimbursement. A strict audit trail of who bought what, why it was an emergency, and how price reasonableness was determined is mandatory.
questions.subject: Procurement Business Principles

questions.q: A standard contract clause that relieves both the agency and the contractor from performing their contractual obligations due to extreme, unforeseeable events (like a hurricane or pandemic) is called:
options: Termination for Convenience
Force Majeure
Indemnification
Liquidated Damages
questions.explain: Force Majeure (Act of God) clauses excuse non-performance when catastrophic, unavoidable events make fulfilling the contract impossible.
questions.subject: Procurement Business Principles

questions.q: During an emergency, an agency utilizes a Time and Materials (T&M) contract for debris removal because the exact scope of work is impossible to define. To remain compliant with federal guidelines, the T&M contract MUST include:
options: A guarantee of a 20% profit margin.
A strict not-to-exceed (NTE) ceiling price.
A geographic preference for local haulers.
An automatic renewal clause.
questions.explain: Under 2 CFR 200, T&M contracts can only be used if no other contract type is suitable, and they must include a strict ceiling price that the contractor exceeds at their own risk.
questions.subject: Procurement Business Principles

questions.q: To mitigate supply chain disruptions during widespread emergencies, an agency should adopt a strategy of:
options: Consolidating all contracts to a single global supplier.
Reducing safety stock to save immediate funds.
Supplier diversification, including maintaining alternative local and regional suppliers.
Relying exclusively on non-contracted spot buys.
questions.explain: Diversifying the supplier base ensures that if one vendor or geographic region is crippled by a disaster, the agency has backup sources to procure essential supplies.
questions.subject: Procurement Business Principles

questions.q: In the Incident Command System (ICS), the procurement and contracting functions typically fall under which major section?
options: Operations Section
Planning Section
Finance / Administration Section
Logistics Section
questions.explain: Under standard ICS structure, Procurement falls under the Finance/Administration section, handling contracts, leases, and documenting costs, working closely with Logistics.
questions.subject: Procurement Business Principles

questions.q: Before awarding a contract utilizing federal emergency funds, the procurement officer MUST verify that the contractor is:
options: Headquartered in the disaster zone.
Not debarred, suspended, or excluded on the federal System for Award Management (SAM.gov).
A certified Disadvantaged Business Enterprise (DBE).
Willing to accept payment via corporate P-Card only.
questions.explain: Federal regulations prohibit agencies from awarding federally funded contracts to vendors who are suspended or debarred. Verifying status on SAM.gov is a mandatory compliance step.
questions.subject: Procurement Business Principles

questions.q: Which action represents the 'Mitigation' phase of disaster management in procurement?
options: Purchasing sandbags as flood waters are actively rising.
Upgrading building infrastructure and relocating a server room out of a flood plain to reduce future risk.
Hiring a debris removal team after the storm has passed.
Applying for FEMA reimbursement grants.
questions.explain: Mitigation involves proactive actions taken before an event occurs to prevent or reduce the long-term impact of future disasters (unlike response or recovery).
questions.subject: Procurement Business Principles

questions.q: When a public agency declares a formal state of emergency, what typically happens to normal competitive bidding thresholds?
options: They are permanently abolished.
They are temporarily waived or increased for purchases directly responding to the emergency.
They are strictly enforced with no exceptions.
They require unanimous approval by the state legislature for every purchase.
questions.explain: An official emergency declaration grants statutory authority to bypass or elevate standard bidding thresholds specifically to expedite the acquisition of goods/services directly necessary to abate the emergency.
questions.subject: Procurement Business Principles

questions.q: To ensure audit readiness for FEMA grants, an agency performs an 'independent cost estimate' (ICE) prior to receiving bids. What is its purpose?
options: To provide vendors with a target price to bid against.
To establish a baseline to determine if the emergency prices received are fair and reasonable.
To calculate the final cost-plus profit margin.
To document the total budget available for the year.
questions.explain: FEMA requires a cost or price analysis for every procurement, including contract modifications. An ICE is developed before receiving bids to evaluate price reasonableness.
questions.subject: Procurement Business Principles
